en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 8.
Cīvarakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Robes)
1. The Story of Jīvaka.
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food.
Seven thousand palaces, seven hundred palaces, and seven palaces;
seven thousand gabled chambers, seven hundred gabled chambers, and seven gabled chambers;
seven thousand parks, seven hundred parks, and seven parks.
There were seven thousand lotus ponds, seven hundred lotus ponds, and seven lotus ponds;
and the courtesan Ambapālī was beautiful, attractive, and pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion,
and skilled in dancing, singing, and instrumental music, sought after by people who desired her.
And as fifty nights passed,
Vesālī became even more resplendent than before.
Then the merchant guild of Rājagaha went to Vesālī on some business or other.
The merchant guild of Rājagaha saw that Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food;
they saw seven thousand palaces, seven hundred palaces, and seven palaces;
and seven thousand gabled houses, seven hundred gabled houses, and seven gabled houses.
Seven thousand parks, seven hundred parks, and seven parks;
seven thousand lotus ponds, seven hundred lotus ponds, and seven lotus ponds;
and the courtesan Ambapālī, who was beautiful, attractive, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.

She was skilled in dancing, singing, and instrumental music; she was sought after by many people who desired her, and she would travel through the night with a retinue of fifty women, making Vesālī even more resplendent.
Then the merchant guild of Rājagaha, having completed their business in Vesālī, returned once again to Rājagaha.
He approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha and, having approached, said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
“Your Majesty, Vesālī is prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food;
it has seven thousand palaces... [and so forth].”
"And because of her, Vesālī shines even more brightly.
'Excellent, Your Majesty! We too shall establish a courtesan.
'In that case, my good man, find such a girl as you might establish as a courtesan.'"
Now at that time, there was in Rājagaha a maiden named Sālavatī, who was beautiful, pleasing to behold, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.
Then the merchant guild of Rājagaha established the maiden Sālavatī as a courtesan.
Before long, the courtesan Sālavatī became skilled in dancing, singing, and instrumental music; she would spend the night for a hundred pieces with whichever men came seeking her service.
Then, before long, the courtesan Sālavatī became pregnant.
Then it occurred to the courtesan Sālavatī:
"A pregnant woman is indeed unpleasant to men."
"If anyone should find out that I,
the courtesan Sālavatī, am pregnant, all my reputation will be ruined.
What if I were to announce that I am ill?"
Then the courtesan Sālavatī commanded her doorkeeper:
"My good doorkeeper, let no man enter.
And if anyone asks for me, report that I am ill."
“Yes, noble lady,” the gatekeeper replied to the courtesan Sālavatī.
Then, as that pregnancy reached its full term, the courtesan Sālavatī gave birth to a son.
Thereupon, the courtesan Sālavatī commanded her maidservant:
“Come now, put this boy in a winnowing basket, carry him out, and throw him away on a rubbish heap.
“Very well, Madam,” the slave girl replied to the courtesan Sālavatī; she put the boy in a winnowing basket, carried him out, and threw him away on a rubbish heap.
Now at that time, a prince named Abhaya, going early in the morning to attend upon the king, saw the boy surrounded by crows. Having seen him, he asked the people:
“What is this, my man, that is surrounded by crows?
“It is a child, Your Majesty.
“Is he alive, my man?”
“He lives, Your Majesty.
“In that case, my good man, take that boy to our inner palace and give him to the nurses to raise.
“Yes, Your Majesty,” those men replied to Prince Abhaya, took the boy to Prince Abhaya’s inner palace, and gave him to the nurses.
"He was nourished," they said;
thus they gave him the name "Jīvaka" (the Living One).
"He was raised by the prince," they said; thus they gave him the name "Komārabhacca" (the Prince's Child).
Then, before long, Jīvaka Komārabhacca reached the age of discretion.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached Prince Abhaya; having approached, he said this to Prince Abhaya:
"Who is my mother, sire, and who is my father?"
“Indeed, my dear Jīvaka, I do not know your mother;
however, I am your father,
for it was by me that you were nourished.”
Then it occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“These royal families cannot easily be supported by means of one’s own craft.
What if I were to train in a craft?”
Now at that time, a world-renowned physician was residing in Takkasilā.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, without taking leave of Prince Abhaya, set out for Takkasilā.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Takkasilā and approached the physician; having approached him, he said this to the physician:
“I wish, teacher, to train in a craft.
“In that case, my dear Jīvaka, you may train,” he said.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca learned much, learned quickly, reflected well upon what he had learned, and did not forget what he had learned.
Then, after seven years had passed, it occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
"I indeed learn much and learn quickly; I retain what I have well learned, and I do not forget what has been learned. Yet, though I have studied for seven years, no end to this craft is in sight.
When will the end of this craft be seen?"
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to that physician and, having approached him, said this to him:

“Teacher, I learn much and I learn quickly; I reflect well upon what I have learned, and I do not forget what has been learned. Yet, though I have studied for seven years, no end to this craft appears.
When will an end to this craft appear?”
“In that case, my dear Jīvaka, take a spade and wander for a league all around Takkasilā; whatever you see that is not a medicine, bring it back.
“Very well, teacher,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to that physician. Taking a spade and wandering for a league all around Takkasilā, he did not see anything that was not a medicine.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to that physician and, having approached him, said this to the physician:
“I have wandered, teacher, for a league all around Takkasilā, yet I did not see anything that was not medicine.
“You are well-trained, my dear Jīvaka;
this is enough for your livelihood,” he said, and gave a small amount of provisions to Jīvaka Komārabhacca.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking that small amount of provisions for the journey, set out for Rājagaha.
Now, while on the road between there and Sāketa, Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s provisions for the journey were completely exhausted.
Then it occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“These roads are indeed wildernesses, lacking water and lacking food; it is not easy to travel them without provisions.
What if I were now to search for provisions?
2. The Story of the Householder’s Wife’s Husband (Seṭṭhibhariyāvatthu)
Now at that time, the merchant’s wife in Sāketa had a head ailment lasting seven years.
Many eminent physicians, renowned throughout the land, came there but were unable to cure her.
They departed, taking with them much gold.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having entered Sāketa, asked the people:
"Who, I say, is sick? Whom shall I treat?
"Teacher, this wife of the guild-president has had a headache for seven years."
“Go, teacher, and treat the merchant’s wife.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to the residence of the householder, the merchant; having arrived, he gave an order to the gatekeeper:
“Go, my good gatekeeper, and inform the merchant’s wife:”
“Madam, the physician has arrived; he wishes to see you.
“Very well, teacher,” the gatekeeper replied to Jīvaka Komārabhacca, and having approached the merchant’s wife, he said to her:
“Madam, the physician has arrived.”
“I wish to see him.
“What is this physician like, my good doorkeeper?
“He is a youth, noble lady.”
“Enough, my good doorkeeper! What will a mere young physician do for me?
Many great and eminent physicians, renowned throughout the regions, have come and were unable to make me well.
They departed taking with them much gold.”
Then that gatekeeper approached Jīvaka Komārabhacca; having approached him, he said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Master, the merchant’s wife says this:
‘Enough, my good gatekeeper! What will a young physician do for me?’”
“Many great and eminent physicians, renowned throughout the land, came and were unable to cure him;
they departed taking with them much gold.
“Go, my good doorkeeper, and tell the guild-president’s wife:”
“The physician, noble lady, says this:
‘Surely, noble lady, you gave nothing away before.
Now that you are healthy, you should give whatever you wish.’”
“Yes, teacher,” the gatekeeper replied to Jīvaka Komārabhacca. He approached the merchant’s wife and, having approached her, said this to the merchant’s wife:
“The physician, noble lady, says thus:
‘Do not, noble lady, give anything away beforehand.’”
“When you have recovered from your illness, you may give whatever you wish.
“In that case, my good doorkeeper, let the physician come,” she said.
“Very well, noble lady,” the doorkeeper replied to the merchant’s wife, and he went to Jīvaka Komārabhacca. Having approached Jīvaka Komārabhacca, he said this to him:
“The merchant’s wife is calling for you, teacher.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to where the merchant’s wife was; having approached and observed her condition, he said this to the merchant’s wife:
“Noble lady, there is need of a pint of ghee.”
Then the merchant’s wife had Jīvaka Komārabhacca administer a handful of ghee.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having prepared that handful of ghee with various medicinal drugs, had the merchant’s wife lie down on her back upon a couch and administered it through the nose.
When that ghee was administered through the nose, it overflowed from her mouth.
Then the merchant’s wife spat into the bowl and commanded her slave-girl:
"Come now, girl, take this ghee with a cotton pad.
Then it occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“It is wonderful how austere this housewife is, in that she will have me take this discarded substance, ghee, with a cotton pad!
And many expensive medicines have been brought for me.
Will she perhaps give me some gift?”
Then the merchant’s wife, having observed Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s change of expression, said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Teacher, why are you dejected?
This thought occurred to me here:
“It is wonderful how frugal this housewife is, that she would have this medicinal ghee—which is of a nature to be discarded—absorbed by a cotton pad!
And many expensive medicines have been brought for me.
Will she perhaps give me some gift?”
“Master, we householders understand this kind of restraint.
It would have been better for this ghee to have been poured as an ointment for the feet of slaves or laborers, or used for lighting lamps.
Do not be distressed, Master.”
“Your gift shall not be diminished.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca removed the seven-year-old head ailment of the guild-president’s wife with a single nasal medication.
When the guild-president’s wife was restored to health, she gave four thousand [pieces] to Jīvaka Komārabhacca.
The son gave four thousand [pieces of gold], thinking, "My mother remains in good health.
The daughter-in-law—
Thinking, “My mother-in-law remains in good health,” he gave four thousand [pieces of gold].
The householder merchant, thinking,
“My wife remains in good health,” gave four thousand [pieces of gold], as well as a male slave, a female slave, and a horse-chariot.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking those sixteen thousand [pieces of gold], along with a male slave, a female slave, and a horse-chariot, set out for Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages, he approached Rājagaha and went to Prince Abhaya; having approached him, he said this to Prince Abhaya:
"Your Majesty, here is my first work: sixteen thousand [pieces of gold], a male slave, a female slave, and a horse-chariot."
“May Your Majesty accept this for my nursing mother.
“Enough, my dear Jīvaka;
let it be yours alone.”
“Build a residence for me right here in our own inner palace.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to Prince Abhaya, and he built a residence for Prince Abhaya within the inner palace.
3. The Story of King Bimbisāra.
Now at that time, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha suffered from hemorrhoids;
his garments were stained with blood.
When the queens saw this, they mocked him.
“The queen is now pregnant; a flower has appeared for the king. It will not be long before the king gives birth.
At this, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha was dejected. Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to Prince Abhaya:
“Indeed, Abhaya, my dear man, I have such an ailment that my garments are stained with blood. When the queens see me, they mock me, saying:
‘The king is now in his season; the flower has appeared on the king; it will not be long before the king gives birth.
Come now, Abhaya, find a physician who might treat me.”
“Your Majesty, this physician Jīvaka of ours is young and excellent.
He will treat Your Majesty.
“In that case, my good Abhaya, summon the physician Jīvaka.”
"He will treat me.
Then Prince Abhaya commanded Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
"Go, my good Jīvaka, and treat the king."
“Yes, sire,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to Prince Abhaya.
Taking some medicine with his fingernail, he went to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, and having approached him,
he said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
“O King, we see that you are afflicted by a disease.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca removed the king’s hemorrhoids, Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha, with a single medicinal ointment.

Thereupon, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha, having recovered his health, had five hundred women adorned with all their ornaments, had them undress, and had them gathered into a heap; he then said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Tell me, Jīvaka, let all these five hundred women’s ornaments be yours.
“Enough, Your Majesty; may Your Majesty remember my service.
“In that case, tell me, Jīvaka, attend upon me, the women’s quarters, and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.”
“Yes, Your Majesty,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Now at that time, the guild-leader of Rājagaha was suffering from a headache for seven years.
Many great and eminent physicians, renowned throughout the land, came but were unable to cure him.
They departed taking with them much gold;
moreover, he was given up by the physicians.
Some physicians said,
"On the fifth day, the householder merchant will pass away.
Other physicians said:
“On the seventh day, the householder merchant will pass away.
Then it occurred to the citizens of Rājagaha:
“This householder merchant has been very helpful to both the king and the citizenry.”
Moreover, he was given up by the physicians.
Some physicians said:
"On the fifth day, the householder merchant will pass away."
Some physicians said,
“On the seventh day, the householder merchant will die.
And this physician Jīvaka of King [Bimbisāra] was young and excellent.
“Perhaps we should now request King Jīvaka the physician to treat the householder Seṭṭhi.
Then the guild of Rājagaha approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha; having approached, they said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
“Sire, this householder Seṭṭhi has been of great benefit both to Your Majesty and to the guild.”
Moreover, he was rejected by the physicians.
Some physicians said:
“On the fifth day, the householder merchant will pass away.”
Some physicians said:
“On the seventh day, the householder merchant will die.
It would be well, Your Majesty, if you were to command the physician Jīvaka to treat the householder merchant.”
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha commanded Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Go, my good Jīvaka, and treat the householder Seṭṭhi.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
He approached the householder merchant; having approached and observed the householder merchant’s condition, he said this to the householder merchant:
"Householder, if you were free from illness, what would be the gift you would give to me?"
“Let all your property be yours, teacher, and I shall be your slave.
“But, householder, will you be able to lie on one side for seven months?
“I am able, teacher, to lie on one side for seven months.”
“But, householder, will you be able to lie on your side for seven months?
“I am able, teacher, to lie on my side for seven months.
“But, householder, will you be able to lie on your back for seven months?”
“I am able, teacher, to lie flat on my back for seven months.

Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca laid the householder merchant upon a couch, secured him to the couch, peeled back the skin of his head, and having opened a suture, he extracted two creatures and showed them to the great crowd:
“Look, sirs, at these two creatures; one is small and one is large.”
Those teachers who said,
"On the fifth day the householder merchant will pass away," have seen this large creature.
On the fifth day, the brain of the householder merchant will be exhausted.
With the exhaustion of the brain, the householder merchant will pass away.
Thus have those teachers been clearly seen by you.
Those teachers who said,
"On the seventh day the householder merchant will pass away," have seen this tiny creature.
"On the seventh day, the brain of the householder merchant will be exhausted.
With the exhaustion of the brain, the householder merchant will pass away.
Thus have those teachers been clearly seen by you."
Having sewn the skin together and stitched the scalp, he applied an ointment.
Then, at the end of seven days, the householder merchant said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
"Teacher, I am not able to lie on one side for seven months."
“Did you not promise me, householder:
‘I am able, teacher, to lie on one side for seven months’?
“It is true, teacher, that I promised; yet I shall die, for I am not able to lie on one side for seven months.”
“In that case, householder, lie on your other side for seven months.
Then, at the end of seven days, the merchant householder said to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Teacher, I am not able to lie on my other side for seven months.”
“Did you not promise me, householder:
‘I am able, teacher, to lie on my right side for seven months’?
“It is true, teacher, that I promised; yet I shall die, teacher, for I am no longer able to lie on my right side for seven months.”
“In that case, householder, lie on your back for seven months.
Then, at the end of seven days, the merchant householder said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Teacher, I am not able to lie on my back for seven months.”
“Did you not promise me, householder:
‘I can, teacher, lie on my back for seven months’?
“It is true, teacher, that I promised; however, I shall die, for I cannot lie on my back for seven months.”
“Householder, if I had not told you this, you would not have recovered even this much; however, I already knew beforehand:
‘In seven days, the householder Seṭṭhi will be free from illness.
Get up, householder! You are well.”
"Do you know what my gift should be?
"Let all your property be yours, teacher, and I myself shall be your slave.
"Enough, householder; do not give me all your property, nor be my slave."
“Give a hundred thousand to the king, and a hundred thousand to me.
Then the householder merchant, having recovered his health, gave a hundred thousand to the king and a hundred thousand to Jīvaka Komārabhacca.
5. The Story of the Merchant’s Son.
Now at that time, a merchant’s son from Bārāṇasī, while playing with a swing, developed a disease of the intestinal knot (*antagaṇṭhābādha*),
because of which even the rice-gruel he drank did not digest properly, nor did the food he ate digest properly,
and his excrement and urine were not discharged normally.
Thus he became emaciated, haggard, discolored, and pale, with veins protruding all over his body.
Then it occurred to the merchant of Bārāṇasī:
"My son has such an affliction that even the gruel he drinks does not digest properly, the food he eats does not digest properly, and even his excrement and urine are not normal."
Thus, because of that, he became emaciated, haggard, discolored, and pale, with his veins showing all over his body.
"What if I were to go to Rājagaha and ask King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha for the physician Jīvaka to treat my son?
Then the merchant of Bārāṇasī went to Rājagaha, approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, and having approached him, said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
“Your Majesty, my son has such an ailment that even the gruel he drinks does not digest properly, and even the food he eats does not digest properly; his excrement and urine are not normal.
Because of this, he is emaciated, haggard, discolored, pale, and his veins stand out all over his body.
It would be well if Your Majesty would command the physician Jīvaka to treat my son.”
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha commanded Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Go, my good Jīvaka, go to Bārāṇasī and treat the guild-president’s son from Bārāṇasī.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Having gone to Bārāṇasī, he approached the merchant’s son of Bārāṇasī; having approached and observed the merchant’s son’s condition,
he cleared away the people, enclosed the area with a curtain, tied him to a pillar,
placed his wife in front of him, tore open his belly, extracted the mass of intestines, and showed them to his wife.

“Look at the illness of your husband: because of it, even the rice-gruel he drinks does not digest properly, and even the food he eats does not digest properly; his excrement and urine are no longer regular.
Because of this, he has become thin, emaciated, discolored, pale and sallow, with veins showing all over his body.
Having untied the intestinal knot, she reinserted the intestines, sewed up the skin of the abdomen, and applied an ointment.
Then, before long, the merchant’s son from Bārāṇasī recovered his health.
Thereupon the merchant of Bārāṇasī, thinking,
“My son is healthy and well,” gave sixteen thousand [pieces of gold] to Jīvaka Komārabhacca.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking those sixteen thousand [pieces of gold], returned once again to Rājagaha.
Now at that time, King Pajjota was afflicted with the disease of jaundice.
Many great and eminent physicians, renowned throughout the land, came but were unable to restore him to health;
they departed taking with them much gold.
Then King Pajjota dispatched a messenger to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, saying:
“I have such an illness; it would be well if the King were to command the physician Jīvaka, for he will treat me.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha commanded Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Go, my good Jīvaka!”
“Go to Ujjain and treat King Pajjota.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Having given his assent, he went to Ujjain and approached King Pajjota; having approached him, [he observed] the King’s ailment.
Having observed King Pajjota, he said this to him:
“Give me ghee, Your Majesty; give me ghee.
I shall cook it, and Your Majesty shall drink it.”
“Enough, my dear Jīvaka; do whatever you can to restore me to health without using ghee.
Ghee is loathsome and repulsive to me.
Then it occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“This king has such an illness that it is not possible to cure him without ghee.
What if I were to cook ghee that has the color of astringent decoctions, the smell of astringent decoctions, and the taste of astringent decoctions?
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca cooked ghee with various medicinal ingredients so that it had the color of astringent decoctions, the smell of astringent decoctions, and the taste of astringent decoctions.
Then it occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
"If this king digests the ghee he has drunk, he will vomit it up.
This king is fierce; he might even have me executed."
"What if I were to ask for permission beforehand?
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached King Pajjota; having approached, he said this to King Pajjota:
"Your Majesty, we who are called physicians extract roots and gather medicines at such a moment's notice."
"Excellent! Let the King command at the stables and at the gates:

'By whatever vehicle Jīvaka desires, by that vehicle let him go; by whichever gate he desires, by that gate let him go; at whatever time he desires, at that time let him go; at whatever time he desires, at that time let him enter.
Then King Pajjota gave orders at the stables and at the gates.
“Let Jīvaka go by whatever vehicle he wishes; let him go through whichever gate he wishes; let him go at whatever time he wishes; let him enter at whatever time he wishes.
Now at that time, King Pajjota had a female elephant named Bhaddavatī who could travel fifty leagues.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca presented ghee to King Pajjota.
“Let the king drink the bitter decoction.
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having made King Pajjota drink the ghee, went to the elephant stable and escaped from the city on the female elephant Bhaddavatikā.
As King Pajjota was digesting that ghee he heaved up a vomit.
Then King Pajjota said this to his men:
"My good men, I have been made to drink ghee by the wicked Jīvaka.
Therefore, my good men, search for the physician Jīvaka."
“Your Majesty, he has departed from the city with the she-elephant Bhaddavatikā.
Now at that time, King Pajjota had a slave named Kāka who could travel sixty yojanas; he was born of a non-human being.
Then King Pajjota commanded the slave Kāka:
“Go, my man Kāka, and bring back the physician Jīvaka, saying:
‘Teacher, the king is having you brought back.
For these physicians, my man Kāka, are indeed full of many deceptions.”
"And do not accept anything from him.
Then Kāka the slave encountered Jīvaka Komārabhacca on the road near Kosambī while he was having his morning meal.
Then Kāka the slave said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“The king is having him turned back, teacher.
“Wait a moment, my man Crow, until we eat.
Come now, my man Crow, let us eat.”
“Enough, teacher; I have been commanded by the king:
‘Tell this crow, my friend, that these so-called physicians are full of many deceptions; do not accept anything from him.
Now at that time, Jīvaka Komārabhacca was picking out medicine with his fingernail, eating an *āmalaka* fruit, and drinking water.”
Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca said this to the slave Kāka:
"Come now, my good Kāka, eat some myrobalan and drink some water.
Then the slave Kāka—
Thinking, “This physician eats the myrobalan fruit and drinks the water; it cannot possibly be harmful,” he ate half a myrobalan fruit and drank some water.
That half-eaten myrobalan fruit was vomited right back up by him.
Then the slave Kāka said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Teacher, will I live?
“Do not fear, my man Kāka; both you and the king shall be free from illness.”
“That king is fierce; he might even have me executed. Therefore, I shall not turn back.
Having entrusted the female elephant Bhaddavatikā to Kāka, he set out for Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages, he approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha; having approached him, he reported this matter to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
“Very well, Jīvaka, you have done well that you did not return; for that king is fierce and might even have had you executed.
Then King Pajjota, having recovered his health, sent a messenger to Jīvaka Komārabhacca, saying:
“Let Jīvaka come; I shall grant him a boon.”
“Enough, noble sir; let His Majesty remember my service.
Now at that time, a pair of garments from Sivi had come into the possession of King Pajjota.

Now at that time, a certain monk was staying alone during the season of the rains.
There, people gave robes, saying, "We give these to the Saṅgha.
Then it occurred to that bhikkhu:
"It has been prescribed by the Blessed One—"
‘The Saṅgha is incomplete by one member.
And I am alone,
as are these people.
Thinking, “We shall give them to the Saṅgha,” they gave the robes.
[The monk thought: “What if I were to take these robes belonging to the Saṅgha to Sāvatthī?
Then that monk, taking those robes, went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the monks.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow you to divide [the robes] by the Saṅgha being present.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk is living alone during the cold season. There, people give robes, saying, ‘We give these to the Saṅgha.’”
“I allow, monks, that monk to determine those robes, saying: ‘These robes are mine.
If, monks, while that robe has not yet been determined by that monk, another monk arrives, an equal share must be given to him.
If, monks, while those monks are dividing that robe and the *kusa*-grass marks have not yet been cast aside, another monk arrives, an equal share must be given to him.”
“If, monks, while that robe-cloth is being distributed by those monks, and the grass has been laid down, another monk arrives, a portion must not be withheld against his will.
Now at that time, two elder brothers, the Venerable Isidāsa and the Venerable Isibhaṭa, having completed the rains residence at Sāvatthī, went to a certain village monastery.
People, thinking, “The elders have come after a long time,” gave them meals along with their robes.
The resident monks asked the elder monks, “Venerable sirs, these robes belonging to the Saṅgha have arisen because of you; will the elders accept a share?
The elders said, “Friends, as we understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those robes belong to you alone until the dismantling of the kaṭhina.
Now at that time, three monks were spending the rains retreat at Rājagaha.
There, people gave robes, saying, "We give these to the Saṅgha.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: "The Blessed One has prescribed that 'the minimum Saṅgha consists of four members.
Yet we are only three persons, and these people are giving robes, saying, 'We give these to the Saṅgha.'"
“How indeed should we proceed?

Now at that time, several elder monks—namely, the Venerable Nīlavāsī, the Venerable Sāṇavāsī, the Venerable Gotaka, the Venerable Bhagu, and the Venerable Phaḷikasantāna—were staying at Pāṭaliputta in the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
Then those monks went to Pāṭaliputta and questioned the elders.
The elders spoke thus:
“Friend, as we understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those robes belong to you alone until the dismantling of the kaṭhina.
22. The Story of Upananda the Sakyan Son.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan had completed the rains retreat at Sāvatthī and went to a certain village monastery.
There, the monks gathered together, desiring to distribute the robes.
They said to him, “Friend, these robes belonging to the Saṅgha are about to be distributed; will you accept a share?”
“Yes, friend, I will accept it.
Then, having taken his share of the robe-cloth, he went to another residence.
There too, the monks gathered together, desiring to divide the robe-cloth.
Then they said to him, “Friend, these robes belonging to the Saṅgha will be distributed; will you accept a share?
“Yes, friends, I will accept,” he replied.
Having taken his share of the robes from there as well, he went to another residence.
There, too, the monks gathered desiring to divide the robes.
They said to him, "Friend, these robes belonging to the Saṅgha are about to be divided; will you accept a share?
"Yes, friends, I will accept it."
Taking a portion of robes from there as well, and carrying a large bundle of robes, he returned once again to Sāvatthī.
The bhikkhus said to him, “Friend Upananda, you are one of great merit; much robe-cloth has accrued to you.
“From where, friends, could I have merit?”
"Here, friends, having spent the rains retreat at Sāvatthī, I went to a certain village monastery.
There, the monks gathered, desiring to distribute the robes.
They said this to me: ‘Friend, these robes belonging to the Saṅgha will be distributed; will you accept a share?’"
“Yes, friend, I will accept it.
Then, having taken my share of the robe-cloth, I went to another residence.
There too, the monks gathered, desiring to distribute the robe-cloth.
Tepi spoke to me thus: “Friend, these robes belonging to the Saṅgha will be distributed; will you consent to take a share?
“Yes, friend, I shall consent,” I replied.
Then, having taken my share of the robes from there as well, I went to another residence.
There too, monks who wished to distribute the robes gathered together.
They also said this to me: “Friend, these robes belonging to the Saṅgha are about to be distributed; will you accept a share?
“Yes, friends, I will accept it.”
“I took a portion of robe-cloth from there as well.
In this way, much robe-cloth has come to me.
“But, friend Upananda, did you consent to a portion of robe-cloth while having spent the rains residence elsewhere?”
“Yes, friends,” they replied.
Then those monks who were few in desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son, having spent the rains residence in one place, accept a share of robe-cloth from another?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
"Is it true, Upananda, that you spent the rains residence in one place and accepted a share of the robe-cloth in another?
"It is true, Blessed One."
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, having spent the rains residence in one place, accept a share of the robe-cloth from another?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the inspiration of those without faith…” [and so on].
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus,
one who has completed the rains residence in one place must not accept a share of robe-cloth from another place.”
“Whoever should consent to it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta was spending the rains retreat alone in two monasteries, thinking, “In this way, much robe-cloth will accrue to me.
Then those monks thought, “How now should the share of robe-cloth be given to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, give that foolish man a single portion.
But in this case, monks, a monk dwells alone for the rains retreat in two residences, thinking: ‘In this way, much robe-cloth will accrue to me.’”
“If he resides half the time here and half the time there, a share of the robe-cloth must be given to him from both places.
Or rather, a share of the robe-cloth must be given from where he resides for the greater part.
23. The Discussion on the Matter of the Sick.
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted with a disease of the stomach.
He lay there, smeared with his own urine and excrement.
Then the Blessed One, with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk, while wandering on a tour of the lodgings, approached the dwelling of that monk.
The Blessed One saw that bhikkhu lying down, submerged in his own urine and excrement. Seeing him, he approached that bhikkhu and, having approached, said to him:
“What is your ailment, bhikkhu?
“I have a stomach disorder, Blessed One.”
“But do you have an attendant, monk?
“No, Blessed One.
“Why don’t the monks attend to you?”
“Venerable sir, I am not a doer for the bhikkhus;
that is why the bhikkhus do not attend upon me.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Go, Ānanda, bring water; we shall bathe this bhikkhu.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One and brought the water.
The Blessed One poured the water.
The Venerable Ānanda washed him.
The Blessed One took hold of him by the head.
The Venerable Ānanda lifted him up by the feet and laid him down on a couch.
Then, on this occasion and for this reason, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Monks, is there a sick monk in such-and-such a monastery?
“There is, Blessed One.”
“Monks, what is that bhikkhu’s ailment?
“Venerable sir, that venerable one has an ailment consisting of a stomach disorder.
“But, monks, does that bhikkhu have an attendant?”
“There is not, Blessed One.
“Why do the bhikkhus not attend upon him?
“Venerable sir, this bhikkhu does nothing for the bhikkhus;”
"Therefore, the monks do not attend upon him.
"Monks, you have no mother, you have no father who might attend upon you.
If you, monks, will not attend upon one another, then who indeed will attend upon you?"
“Monks, whoever would attend upon me should attend upon the sick.
If he has a preceptor, he should be attended upon by the preceptor for as long as life lasts;
his recovery must be awaited.”
If there is a teacher, he should be attended upon by the pupil for as long as life lasts;
one must wait for his recovery.
If there is a co-resident student, he should be attended upon by the teacher for as long as life lasts.
One must wait for his recovery.
If he has a resident pupil, that pupil must attend upon him for as long as life lasts;
one must wait for his recovery.
If he has a common preceptor, he should attend upon his common preceptor for as long as life lasts;
he should wait for his recovery.
If he has a common teacher, he should attend upon his common teacher for as long as life lasts.
One must wait for his recovery.
If there is no preceptor, teacher, co-resident, pupil, fellow-preceptor, or fellow-teacher, he should be attended by the Saṅgha.
If one does not attend him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“Monks, a patient endowed with five factors is difficult to attend to: he does what is unwholesome;
he does not know moderation regarding what is wholesome; he does not take his medicine;
he does not describe his illness as it truly is to the attendant who desires his welfare, saying, ‘When I am moving forward, I am moving forward’;”

When one who is walking back perceives him as "he is walking back," or when one who is standing perceives him as "he is standing," such a person is by nature unable to endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful,
sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
Possessing these five factors, monks, a patient is difficult to attend to.
“Monks, a patient endowed with five factors is well attended:
he does what is beneficial; he knows the proper measure regarding what is beneficial; he takes his medicine;
he reveals the illness as it truly is to the attendant who desires his welfare, saying, ‘When it advances, it advances,’ and so forth.”
When one who is walking back perceives: "He is walking back," or when one who is standing perceives:
"He is standing," he is one who is by nature patient toward arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
It is with these five factors, monks, that a patient is well-supported.
“Monks, a nurse endowed with five qualities is not fit to attend to the sick:
he is not capable of providing medicine; he does not know what is suitable and what is unsuitable; he offers what is unsuitable and withdraws what is suitable;
he attends to the sick for the sake of material gain and not out of a mind of loving-kindness; and he is disgusted by excrement.”
or urine, or spittle, or vomit; nor is he able from time to time to instruct, exhort, inspire, and gladden the sick person with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a nurse is not fit to attend to the sick.
“Monks, a nurse endowed with five qualities is capable of attending to the sick:
he is able to provide medicine; he knows what is suitable and what is unsuitable; he sets aside what is unsuitable and provides what is suitable;
he attends to the sick with a mind of loving-kindness and not for the sake of material gain; and he is not disgusted by excrement.”
or urine, or spittle, or vomit; he is capable of instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the sick from time to time with a talk on the Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a nurse is fit to attend to the sick.”
24. The Story of What Belongs to the Dead.
Now at that time, two monks were traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
They arrived at a certain monastery.
There, a certain bhikkhu was sick.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, the Blessed One has praised attendance upon the sick."
"Come, friends, let us attend to this bhikkhu.
They attended to him.
While being attended to by them, he passed away.
Then those monks, taking that monk’s bowl and robe, went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, when a monk has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robe;
however, those who attended to the sick have been of great assistance.”
“I allow, monks, for the Saṅgha to give a set of three robes and a bowl to those who have attended to the sick.
And this, monks, is how it should be given.
That monk who has attended to the sick, having approached the Saṅgha, should speak thus:”
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhu named so-and-so has passed away.
This is his triple robe and his bowl.
A competent and capable bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
The bhikkhu named so-and-so has passed away.
This is his triple robe and his bowl.’
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this triple robe and bowl to the attendants of the sick.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
The bhikkhu named so-and-so has passed away.
This is his triple robe and his bowl.
The Sangha gives this triple robe and bowl to those who attended upon him while he was ill.
Whichever venerable one approves of this gift of the triple robe and the bowl to the attendants of the sick, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
This triple robe and bowl have been given by the Saṅgha to the attendants of the sick.
"It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this to be so.
Now at that time, a certain novice had passed away.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, when a novice has died, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes;
however, those who attended to him while he was ill have been of great service.
Monks, I allow that the Saṅgha give both the robe and the bowl to those who attended to the novice while he was ill.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be given in this way:
That monk who has been attending to the sick should approach the Saṅgha and speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, the novice named so-and-so has passed away; here is his robe and his bowl.”
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
The novice named so-and-so has passed away."
This is his robe and bowl.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe and bowl to those who attended upon the sick.
This is the motion.
Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
The novice named so-and-so has passed away.
This is his robe and his bowl.
The Saṅgha gives this robe and this bowl to the attendants of the sick.
Whichever venerable one approves of the giving of this robe and this bowl to the attendants of the sick, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“This robe and bowl have been given by the Saṅgha to the attendants of the sick.
It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Now at that time, a certain monk and a novice were attending to a sick person.
While being attended by them in this way, he passed away.
Then, it occurred to that monk who had been his attendant during the illness:
“How now should a share of the robe-cloth be given to the novice who attended me while I was ill?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to give an equal share to the novice who has been attending to the sick.
Now at that time, a certain monk who possessed many goods and many requisites passed away.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, when a monk has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes;
nevertheless, those who attended to him while he was ill were of great assistance.”
“I allow you, monks, for the Saṅgha to give the three robes and the bowl to those who have attended to the sick.
Whatever light goods or light requisites there are, that may be distributed by the Saṅgha present.
Whatever heavy goods or heavy requisites there are, that is not to be sold nor divided, but belongs to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, past and future.”
25. The Discourse on the Prohibition of Nakedness Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One while naked; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, the Blessed One in many ways speaks in praise of fewness of wishes, of contentment, of effacement, of the ascetic practices, of inspiring confidence, of reduction [of worldly things], and of the arousal of energy. Yet, venerable sir, I am naked.”

“Venerable sir, this nakedness leads in many ways to fewness of wishes, to contentment, to effacement, to the ascetic practices, to inspiring confidence, to the reduction of worldly concerns, and to the arousal of energy.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would allow nakedness for the bhikkhus.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unbecoming, foolish man, it is unsuitable, it is unworthy, it is unbefitting a recluse, it is improper, and it is not to be done.
How indeed, foolish man, could you undertake the nakedness of a sectarian?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so forth].”
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, one should not adopt the nakedness of the ascetics.”
“Whoever should take it up, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
26. Discussion on the Prohibition of Grass Garments, etc.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, having dressed himself in a grass garment... [and so forth].
Having clothed himself in a garment of bark...
having clothed himself in a garment of wood-shavings...
having clothed himself in a blanket of hair... [and so forth].
Having put on a hair-blanket …pe… having put on an owl’s wing …pe… having put on a deerskin cloak.
He approached the Blessed One and, having approached, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, in many ways the Blessed One speaks in praise of fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, asceticism, serenity, reduction, and the arousal of energy.
Venerable sir, this antelope skin leads in many ways to fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, asceticism, serenity, reduction, and the arousal of energy.”
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would allow the monks to wear a cloak of antelope skin.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unseemly, foolish man, it is unbecoming, it is unsuitable, it is unworthy of a recluse, it is improper, and it is not to be done.”
"How indeed, foolish man, can you wear an antelope skin, the banner of the sectarians?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on]...
Having rebuked him..."
Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, one must not wear a deer-skin cloak, which is the emblem of the sectarians.
Whoever should wear one commits a thullaccaya offense.”

Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, having dressed himself in a garment made of reed-tubes … [and] having dressed himself in a garment made of bark, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, in many ways the Blessed One speaks in praise of fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, the ascetic practices, serenity, reduction, and the arousal of energy. Yet here I am, having dressed myself in a garment made of reed-tubes … [and] having dressed myself in a garment made of bark.”

“Venerable sir, this cloth matting, in many ways, leads to fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, the ascetic practices, inspiring confidence, the reduction of acquisitions, and the arousal of energy.
It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would allow the cloth matting for the bhikkhus.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unseemly, foolish man, it is unbecoming, it is improper, it is unworthy of a recluse, it is not allowable, it is not to be done.
How can you, foolish man, wear a cloth as an undergarment?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without faith …” [and so on].
Having rebuked him … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, a cotton cloth must not be worn as an undergarment.”
Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
27. Discussion of the Prohibition Against All-Blue and Other [Colored] Robes:
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks wore robes that were entirely blue... [etc.]
They wear robes that are entirely yellow …pe… they wear robes that are entirely red …pe… they wear robes that are entirely madder-colored …pe…
They wear robes that are entirely black …pe… they wear robes dyed entirely with madder …pe… they wear robes dyed entirely with mahānāma …pe…
They wear robes with uncut fringes …pe… they wear robes with long fringes …pe… they wear robes with floral fringes …pe…
They wear robes with hoods …pe… they wear tunics …pe… they wear tirīṭaka garments …pe…
They wore turbans.
People criticized, complained, and grumbled, saying,
"How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, wear turbans just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, robes that are entirely blue should not be worn; robes that are entirely yellow should not be worn;
robes that are entirely red should not be worn; robes that are entirely madder-red should not be worn.”
One should not wear robes that are entirely black; one should not wear robes dyed with all-red lac;
one should not wear robes dyed with all-yellow *mahānāma* (turmeric); one should not wear robes with uncut fringes; one should not wear robes with long fringes;
one should not wear robes with floral fringes; nor should one wear robes with serpent-hood fringes.
“Robes are to be worn; a bodice is not to be worn, a tirīṭaka garment is not to be worn, nor a turban is to be worn.
Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
28. Discussion on those who have completed the rains residence having no robe-cloth yet arisen.
Now at that time, monks who had completed the rains retreat departed while robes had not yet been produced;
some disrobed, some died, some claimed to be novices, some claimed to have renounced the training, some claimed to have committed an offense involving defeat,
some claimed to be insane, some claimed to be deranged, and some claimed to be overwhelmed by pain.
They claim [to be monks]; those suspended for not seeing an offense also claim [to be monks]; those suspended for not making amends for an offense also claim [to be monks];
those suspended for not relinquishing a pernicious view also claim [to be monks];

eunuchs also claim [to be monks]; those living in the community by theft also claim [to be monks]; those who have gone over to another sect also claim [to be monks]; even animals also claim [to be monks].
They claim [to be such]; they also claim to be matricides, they also claim to be patricides, they also claim to be murderers of Arhats,
they also claim to be violators of nuns, they also claim to be schismatics of the Saṅgha, they also claim to be shedders of blood [of an Arhat],
and they also claim to be hermaphrodites.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“In this case, monks, if a monk who has completed the rains retreat departs while the robe-cloth has not yet been produced, it should be given provided there is a suitable recipient.
In this case, monks, if a monk who has completed the rains retreat disrobes or passes away while the robe-cloth has not yet been produced...”
If he admits to being a novice, if he admits to having renounced the training, or if he admits to having committed an offense involving defeat,
the Saṅgha is the master. But here, monks,
a monk who has completed the rains residence, when robes have not yet arisen, admits to being insane.
One who admits while deranged, one who admits while overwhelmed by pain, one suspended for not seeing an offense,
one suspended for not making amends for an offense, or one suspended for not relinquishing a pernicious view—
[the robe] should be given if there is a suitable person to receive it.
But here, monks, a monk who has completed the rains residence, when robe-cloth has not yet arisen, claims to be a paṇḍaka; claims to be one living in communion by theft;
claims to have gone over to another sect; claims to be an animal; claims to be a matricide;
claims to be a patricide; claims to be a murderer of an arahant; claims to be a defiler of a bhikkhunī; or...

One who confesses to being a schismatic in the Saṅgha, one who confesses to causing the shedding of blood [from a Tathāgata], or one who confesses to being a hermaphrodite—the Saṅgha is the owner [of the robe].
But here, monks, when a monk who has completed the rains residence departs while the robe-cloth has arisen but not yet been distributed, it should be given if there is a suitable recipient.
But here, monks, when a monk who has completed the rains residence disrobes while the robe-cloth has arisen but not yet been distributed, or dies—
[If] he acts [as such], and the novice admits it; if one who has renounced the training admits it; if one who has committed an offense involving defeat admits it—the Saṅgha is the authority.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk who has completed the rains residence, when robe-cloth has arisen but not yet been distributed, admits that he is insane.
One who admits while distracted admits; one who admits while overwhelmed by pain admits; one suspended for not seeing an offense admits;
one suspended for not making amends for an offense admits; one suspended for not relinquishing a wrong view admits.
It should be given when there is a suitable recipient.
"Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk who has completed the rains residence, while the robe-cloth has arisen but not yet been distributed, claims to be a paṇḍaka;
or claims to be one living in communion by theft; or claims to have gone over to another sect; or claims to be an animal; or claims to be a matricide;
or claims to be a patricide; or claims to be a murderer of an arahant; or claims to be a defiler of a bhikkhunī."
He confesses; he confesses as one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha; he confesses as one who has shed blood [of a Buddha]; he confesses as one who is a hermaphrodite.
The Saṅgha is the master. 29.
Discussion on the Arising of Robes when the Saṅgha is Divided.
But here, monks, while the robe-cloth has not yet arisen for the monks who have completed the rains residence, the Saṅgha becomes divided. There,
people give water to one faction and robe-cloth to the other faction,
saying, "We give it to the Saṅgha."
This belongs to the Saṅgha alone.
Furthermore, monks, when the robe-cloth has not yet been offered to monks who have completed the rains residence, the Saṅgha becomes divided.
In that case, people give water to one faction and give robe-cloth to that very same faction.
"We give it to the Sangha.
This belongs to the Sangha alone.
But here, monks, while the robes have not yet been distributed for the monks who have completed the rains residence, the Sangha becomes divided.
In that regard, people give water to one faction and robes to the other faction,
saying, "We give to the faction.
This belongs to the faction itself.
"Furthermore, monks, suppose that while the robe-material has not yet arisen for the monks who have completed the rains residence, the Saṅgha becomes split. There,
people give water to one faction and give robe-material to that very same faction, saying,
'We give it to the faction.'"
“This applies to the fortnight.
But in this case, monks, when the robe-cloth has arisen for monks who have completed the rains residence and it has not yet been distributed, and the Saṅgha becomes split,
it must be distributed equally among all.”
30. Discussion on What is Misunderstood and What is Well-Understood Now at that time, the Venerable Revata sent a robe for the Venerable Sāriputta into the hand of a certain bhikkhu, saying:
"Give this robe to the Elder."
Then, on the way, that bhikkhu took that robe cloth out of trust in the Venerable Revata.
When the Venerable Revata had met with the Venerable Sāriputta, he asked:
"Venerable sir, I sent a robe for the Elder."
“Have you received that robe?
“I do not see that robe, friend.
Then the Venerable Revata said this to that bhikkhu:
“Friend, I sent a robe for the Elder into the Venerable’s hands.
Where is that robe?
